readerTitle: Why McDonald's collects rent from its own restaurants
caseNote: 실제 기업 (McDonald's, 1950년대 Ray Kroc와 Harry Sonneborn의 부동산 모델) + 가상 적용 (철물점 프랜차이즈)
insight: 고객이 사는 것과 사업이 버는 방식은 다를 수 있다. 가장 단단한 수익원은 고객 눈에 보이지 않는 층에 있을 때가 많다.
misconception: 햄버거 회사는 햄버거를 팔아서 돈을 번다. 프랜차이즈 본사의 수입은 로열티가 전부다.

sources.text: Ray Kroc with Robert Anderson, Grinding It Out: The Making of McDonald's (1977) — 맥도날드 형제와의 초기 계약 조건(1.9% 서비스 수수료), Sonneborn의 부동산 아이디어
John F. Love, McDonald's: Behind the Arches (1986) — Harry Sonneborn, Franchise Realty Corporation(1956) 설립과 임대 구조
McDonald's Corporation, Form 10-K annual reports (SEC EDGAR) — 가맹점 비율, 가맹점 수입 구성(임대료·로열티·가맹비), 매출 연동 임대료 구조

factChecks.note: 초기 계약의 서비스 수수료 1.9%(그중 0.5%가 맥도날드 형제 몫)는 Kroc의 자서전과 Love(1986)에 나옵니다. 게시 전 원문으로 재확인하세요. 카드에는 1.9%만 적었습니다.
Franchise Realty Corporation 설립 연도 1956년과 Harry Sonneborn의 역할은 Love(1986)로 확인하세요. Sonneborn의 유명한 '우리는 부동산 사업을 한다' 발언은 정확한 문구가 자료마다 달라 직접 인용하지 않고 풀어 썼습니다.
가맹점 비율 '약 95%'는 최근 10-K(2023~2024년) 기준입니다. 게시 직전 최신 10-K로 다시 확인하세요.
10-K에는 가맹점 임대료가 대체로 매출의 일정 비율에 최저 임대료를 더한 구조라고 나옵니다. 임대료가 로열티보다 큰지 여부는 연도별 수치를 확인한 뒤에만 쓰세요. 카드에는 'one of its largest sources of income'으로만 적었습니다.
임대 계약을 통해 기준 미준수 가맹점을 통제할 수 있었다는 설명은 Kroc 자서전과 Love(1986)의 서술에 근거합니다. 원문 표현을 확인하세요.
철물점 사례는 설명용 가상 사례이며 수치는 없습니다.

cards.title: Why McDonald's collects rent from its own restaurants
body: Most McDonald's restaurants are run by independent owners, not by the company itself. Those owners sell the burgers.
So where does McDonald's make its money? A big part of the answer is the ground under the restaurant. In many cases, the owner's landlord is McDonald's.

image.label: A burger restaurant sitting on a plot of land with a lease document
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 패스트푸드 매장이 잔디 땅 조각 위에 놓여 있고, 땅 아래쪽에 '임대 계약서' 문서가 뿌리처럼 깔려 있음. 실제 맥도날드 로고, 골든 아치, 상표 색 조합은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You're Ray Kroc in the mid-1950s.
body: Kroc had the rights to franchise the McDonald brothers' restaurant. But his deal capped what he could charge: a service fee of 1.9% of each restaurant's sales. Growth was fast, cash was thin, and some owners cut corners on quality.
How would you fix the business?

options.text: Push for a higher fee on each restaurant's sales
options.feedback: More income per restaurant, if the brothers and owners agree. But the contract limited fees, and a bigger fee does nothing to stop owners cutting corners.

options.text: Stop franchising and open only company-run restaurants
options.feedback: You'd control quality and keep all the profit. But each restaurant needs your money and managers, and Kroc had little of either. Growth would crawl.

options.text: Secure the land and buildings, then rent them to the owners
options.feedback: This adds a second income stream the fee cap didn't touch, and the lease gives you leverage over standards. It costs capital and debt, as later cards show.

cards.title: A finance man found a second business.
body: Harry Sonneborn, Kroc's finance chief, proposed the real estate route. In 1956 they set up a company, Franchise Realty Corporation, to lease or buy restaurant sites and then rent them to franchisees at a higher price.
The owner now paid McDonald's twice: a fee on sales, and rent. And the lease mattered. An owner who ignored the standards could lose the building, not just the brand.
Sonneborn reportedly liked to say McDonald's was really in the real estate business.

cards.title: Revenue streams can sit in different layers
body: A **revenue stream** is one distinct way a business collects money. One business can have several, from different customers or different things it provides.
Customers see McDonald's selling food. But the franchise owner is also a customer, buying a brand, a system and a location. Each of those can carry its own price.

image.label: Three stacked layers: food, brand fee, rent
image.brief: 단면 인포그래픽. 맨 위 층 'Food: customer pays owner', 가운데 층 'Brand and system: owner pays a fee', 맨 아래 가장 두꺼운 층 'Land and building: owner pays rent'. 로고 없음.

cards.softwareNote: Software has the same layers. A tool customers know for its features may earn most of its money from payments it processes or data storage underneath, not from the subscription on the price page.

cards.title: One restaurant, several streams.
body: Today about 95% of McDonald's restaurants are franchised, according to its annual reports. Rent from those owners is **one of its largest sources of income**.

breakdown.label: Customer → owner
breakdown.detail: The owner keeps the sales and pays staff and supplies

breakdown.label: Owner → McDonald's
breakdown.detail: A royalty based on a share of sales

breakdown.label: Owner → McDonald's
breakdown.detail: Usually a minimum plus a share of sales

cards.title: Rent is steadier than burgers.
body: The owner carries the daily risk: wages, food costs, a bad month. McDonald's collects rent with a minimum floor, and it rises when sales rise.
The streams also support each other. A strong brand brings traffic. Traffic makes the sites valuable. Valuable sites give McDonald's more control over the owners who run them.

cards.title: This stream has a price.
body: Owning or leasing thousands of sites makes the business **asset-heavy**. It needs capital and often debt, and property values can fall.

The rent also only works because the restaurants succeed. A weak brand makes empty buildings. And when rent rises faster than an owner's profit, the landlord and the tenant start pulling in opposite directions.

cards.title: Now it's a hardware store chain.
body: You've built a popular neighborhood hardware brand and are letting independent owners open stores under your name. You charge a small fee on their sales. Some owners let their stores get messy, and your income swings with their results.

options.text: Raise the fee on sales for every owner
options.feedback: More income, but the same single stream with the same swings. It also squeezes owners without giving you more say over standards.

options.text: Lease good sites yourself and rent them to owners, with rent tied to sales and clear standards
options.feedback: You add a steadier stream and real leverage. The cost is long leases on your books, so pick sites you'd be happy to stand behind.

options.text: Borrow heavily and buy every store building outright, fast
options.feedback: You'd own valuable property, but a slow year for the brand could leave you with debt and empty shops. Asset-heavy works best built carefully.

cards.title: What customers buy isn't always how you earn.
body: McDonald's sells burgers to customers and locations to owners. The quieter stream made the business stronger.
**Try it today:** list everyone who pays your business, and for what. Is there a layer, such as space, equipment or access, you provide but don't charge for?
